title: Pet routines, feeding and medication
audience: Pet sitters who feed, exercise, medicate and check animals in the owner's home or at another property
referencesAtStart: Official source: Agriculture Victoria, Code of Practice for the Operation of Boarding Establishments (revision 1, updated October 2004; printed April 2025), which applies to boarding establishments.
learningOutcomes: Follow the owner's written routine for feeding, exercise, toileting and rest, and record each step
Give medication only as the owner and the vet have directed, and record each dose
Recognise the signs of illness or distress that need an immediate call to the owner or vet

instruction.heading: The owner's written routine is the standard
instruction.body: A pet sitter follows the owner's written routine, not the sitter's own habits. The routine covers meals and portion sizes, the food brand, feeding times, walks and toileting, play, rest, litter or cage care, and any special needs such as a diet or a behaviour plan. Before the first visit, confirm each item with the owner, and record the answers in the client file. Where the owner's routine conflicts with the sitter's view of what is good for the animal, the sitter follows the routine and raises the concern with the owner. A change to the routine needs the owner's written agreement. The business's routine record is held in {{business:procedures.approved_sop}}.

instruction.heading: Medication: only as directed, and recorded
instruction.body: Medication is a high-risk task. Give medication only where the owner's written instructions and the vet's directions match, and where the dose, the timing and the method are clear. Check the label of the medicine against the instructions before each dose, and record each dose with the time given. Never give a human medicine to an animal, and never double a dose to catch up on a missed one unless the vet's written direction says to. Where a dose is missed or the animal refuses it, call the owner or the vet for guidance and record the call. The business should not give any medication until the owner has provided written direction, and until the business procedure has been followed.

instruction.heading: Signs of illness and when to call
instruction.body: A sitter must watch each animal at every visit for changes from its normal behaviour. Signs that need an immediate call to the owner or the vet include vomiting or diarrhoea that does not stop, refusal of food or water for a period the vet has set, difficulty breathing, collapse, a seizure, bleeding, a limp that stops the animal walking, a swollen abdomen, and any sudden change in behaviour that is severe. Where the owner cannot be reached, call the vet named in the owner's written authority. The emergency steps for animal first response are set out in “Pet first aid and emergency vet referral”, and the owner's authority to take the animal to care must be on the file before any visit.

procedure: Confirm each item of the owner's routine in writing before the first visit, and record the answers
Follow the routine at each visit, and record each feed, walk, toilet break and medication dose with the time
Check the medicine label against the owner's written instructions and the vet's direction before each dose
Never give a human medicine, and never double a dose without the vet's written direction
Watch each animal for changes at every visit, and record the observations
Call the owner or the vet at once for any serious sign, and record the call and the advice given

workedExamples.situation: A sitter is looking after a cat that needs a tablet twice a day. The owner's note says 'give one tablet each morning and evening'. The sitter finds the cat has refused the evening dose.
workedExamples.reasoning: The owner's written routine is clear that the dose is given twice a day, and the sitter has a missed dose. The sitter should not double the next dose unless the vet's written direction says so. The sitter should call the owner or the vet for guidance, record the refusal and the call, and follow the advice. The sitter should not give a human medicine as a substitute.

workedExamples.situation: A dog's owner has left a routine that says the dog should have two walks a day. On the second day, the dog is slow to get up and has not eaten its breakfast.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: Should the sitter follow the routine and walk the dog?
workedExamples.reasoning: A dog that is slow to rise and not eating is showing a change from normal behaviour. The sitter should not push the walk as the routine says. The sitter should record the observations, call the owner and the vet, and follow their advice before any walk. The routine is followed where it is safe, and a change in health takes priority.

equipmentAndPpe: Owner's written routine, held in the client file
Medicine record with the label check and the dose log
Gloves for handling medicine and for cleaning litter or waste
Phone with the owner's and the vet's contact details

commonErrors.error: Doubling a missed dose to catch up.
commonErrors.prevention: Call the owner or the vet for guidance. Do not double a dose unless the vet's written direction says so.

commonErrors.error: Giving a human medicine because it worked for the sitter's own pet.
commonErrors.prevention: Never give a human medicine to an animal.

commonErrors.error: Following the routine when the animal shows a change in health.
commonErrors.prevention: Record the change, call the owner and vet, and follow their advice before continuing the routine.

commonErrors.error: Skipping the dose log because the sitter remembers it.
commonErrors.prevention: Record every dose with the time at the moment it is given.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: The rule for who may give medication to a pet, in each state, was not researched. The business should give medication only on written owner and vet direction.
The Victorian boarding code requires boarding establishments to hold a signed arrangement with vets on call (section 4.2).
Completing this lesson does not grant any authority to prescribe, administer or change treatment for an animal.

qualityStandard: Every visit follows the owner's written routine, and each step is recorded
Every medication dose is recorded with the time, the label check and the method
No human medicine is given to any animal
Every serious sign is recorded, with the owner or vet call and the advice given
documentationEvidence: Owner's written routine, dated and signed or confirmed
Visit log with feeds, walks, toilet breaks and observations
Medication dose log with label check, time and method
Record of each call to the owner or vet, and the advice given
summary: Follow the owner's written routine, and record each step
Give medication only on written owner and vet direction; never give human medicine
Watch for changes at every visit and call the owner or vet at once for serious signs
Completing this lesson grants no authority to prescribe or treat
referencesAtEnd: Official source, as listed at the start: Agriculture Victoria, Code of Practice for the Operation of Boarding Establishments.

knowledgeChecks.question: A cat refuses its evening dose of a tablet. What is the correct action?
options: Call the owner or vet for guidance, and record the refusal and the call
Double the next morning dose to catch up on the missed dose quickly
Give a human medicine that the sitter has at home to help the cat

knowledgeChecks.question: A dog is slow to rise and has not eaten its breakfast. The routine says to walk it twice a day. What should the sitter do?
options: Walk the dog as the routine says, since routines are fixed and the owner expects it
Record the observations, call the owner and vet, and follow their advice before any walk
Give the dog extra food to help it recover, since eating is the best sign of health

knowledgeChecks.question: Whose routine does a pet sitter follow?
options: The routine from the last sitter
